old: Digital tracking with decision support or reminders probably makes little or no difference to some types of health outcomes, but its effect on other outcomes, including maternal and neonatal deaths, is uncertain because the evidence is very low-certainty [2].
new: Mobile phone-based decision-support tools probably make little or no difference to some types of health outcomes, but their effect on other outcomes, including maternal and neonatal deaths, is uncertain because the evidence is very low-certainty [2].

old: The effect of digital tracking with decision support and/or client reminders on health service use is unknown because no studies were found [3].

Based on 10 trials, mobile tracking of clients' care with decision support or reminders (TCCMD) may modestly increase health service use such as vaccinations and HIV care (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.34; low-certainty evidence), though effects varied widely between studies [3].
new: Based on 10 trials, targeted client communication via mobile devices (TCCMD), such as text messages reminding parents of children under five to attend appointments or offering health information, may modestly increase health service use such as vaccinations and HIV care compared with standard care (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.34; low-certainty evidence), though effects varied widely between studies [3].

old: Tracking combined with communication on mobile devices may increase antenatal appointment attendance (OR 1.54, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.96), but this is low-certainty evidence and the confidence interval includes both benefit and harm [3].
new: Targeted client communication via mobile devices (TCCMD) may increase antenatal appointment attendance (OR 1.54, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.96), but this is low-certainty evidence and the confidence interval includes both benefit and harm [3].

old: The effect of digital tracking with decision support and/or client messaging on the proportion of births occurring in a health facility is uncertain, because the evidence is of very low certainty [3].
new: Among pregnant and postpartum women living with HIV, the effect of targeted client communication via mobile devices, compared with standard care, on the proportion of births occurring in a health facility is uncertain, because the evidence is of very low certainty [3].

old: No studies reported on maternal mortality or morbidity, so the effect of these mobile tracking and prompt or reminder interventions on those outcomes is unknown [3].
new: For pregnant and postpartum women living with HIV, no studies reported on maternal mortality or morbidity, so the effect of these mobile tracking and prompt or reminder interventions on those outcomes in this group is unknown [3].

old: The effect of digital targeted client communication via mobile devices compared with non-digital targeted client communication is unknown, because no studies reported this comparison [3].
new: Compared with non-digital targeted client communication (e.g. pamphlets), digital targeted client communication via mobile devices may have little or no effect on exclusive breastfeeding (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.07) and may reduce 'any maternal health problem' reported up to 10 days postpartum (RR 0.19, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.79) (low-certainty evidence); its effect on health service use, and for some other groups of participants on any outcome, is unknown because no studies reported it [3].

old: No trials in any population reported data on unintended consequences of these mobile tracking, decision-support and reminder interventions, so potential harms remain unmeasured [3].
new: No trials in any population reported data on unintended consequences of targeted client communication via mobile devices, so potential harms remain unmeasured [3].

old: For pregnant and postpartum women living with HIV, mobile-device tracking combined with client communication (TCCMD) may make little or no difference to maternal and infant adherence to antiretroviral therapy compared with standard care (low-certainty evidence) [3].
new: For pregnant and postpartum women living with HIV, TCCMD may make little or no difference to maternal and infant adherence to antiretroviral therapy compared with standard care (low-certainty evidence) [3].

old: Digital tracking with provider prompts or client messages may reduce sexually transmitted infection rates (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.33), but this is low-certainty evidence and the interval includes both benefit and harm [4].
new: Among adolescents, targeted text-message communication via mobile devices, compared with digital non-targeted communication, may reduce chlamydia or gonorrhoea incidence (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.33), but this is low-certainty evidence from a single underpowered pilot trial of 200 young people in Britain, and the interval includes both benefit and harm [4].

old: No study measured the impact of this intervention on sexually transmitted infection (STI) rates, so its effect on that health outcome is unknown [4].
new: For adult populations, no study measured the impact of this intervention compared with standard care on sexually transmitted infection (STI) rates, so its effect on that outcome is unknown for this comparison [4].

old: The effect of mobile tracking with decision support and/or client messages on condom use is uncertain [4].
new: The effect of targeted client communication via mobile devices (TCCMD) on condom use is uncertain, whether compared with standard care or with digital non-targeted communication [4].

old: For health outcomes, mobile tracking with prompts or reminders may have little or no effect on CD4 count (mean difference 13.99, 95% CI -8.65 to 36.63) and may slightly reduce virological failure (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.01), both low-certainty evidence [4].
new: For health outcomes in adults living with HIV, targeted client communication via mobile devices may have little or no effect on CD4 count (mean difference 13.99 cells per mm3, 95% CI -8.65 to 36.63; three trials in China and Cameroon) and may slightly reduce virological failure (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.01; two trials in Kenya and India), both low-certainty evidence [4].

old: For digital tracking with client communication on mobile devices versus non-digital tracking and communication, no studies reported STI rates, condom use, ART adherence, abortion rates, or contraceptive use, so effects on these outcomes are unknown [4].
new: For targeted client communication via mobile devices (TCCMD) versus non-digital targeted client communication, no studies reported STI rates, condom use, ART adherence, abortion rates, or contraceptive use; TCCMD may modestly increase service attendance overall (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.35; low-certainty evidence), though the confidence interval encompasses benefit and harm [4].
Of the 18 eligible studies, 11 were randomised and seven non-randomised, and they were conducted in Bangladesh, China, Ethiopia, India, Kenya, Palestine, Uganda, and the USA [1].

The review authors add that they have "little confidence in the findings because there were not many studies; some studies were small, and others had design problems that made their findings less certain" [1].
